implementation_notes: Boost.Asio ships the initiation dispatcher: io_context provides an event processing loop, and its documentation is explicit that run()/poll() must be called for asynchronous operations to progress and that handlers are invoked only by a thread currently calling one of those functions. Sockets, acceptors and deadline_timer are the handles, and the async_* calls carry the handler that the loop dispatches, so the handle-to-handler registry collapses into per-operation completion handlers plus session objects that re-issue the next operation. Two members replace the classic structure explicitly: a strand serialises handler execution so several threads may run one io_context without locking per-session state, and a work guard keeps run() from returning when there is temporarily nothing to do. Write a loop by hand only to integrate a foreign event source through a custom service.
pitfalls: Running blocking work inside a completion handler stalls every operation on that io_context; a handler must re-issue the next async operation and return.
The loop stops when it runs out of work, so a long-lived service needs a work guard (or an outstanding async operation), otherwise run() returns and the server silently exits.

With several threads calling run() on one io_context the handlers may execute concurrently; session state must be posted to the session's strand instead of being touched directly in the completion handler.

variants.name: ACE_Reactor and ACE_Event_Handler (classic POSA2 realization)
variants.implementation_notes: ACE is where the pattern was first described (POSA2, and C++ Network Programming volume 2 whose chapters 3 and 4 cover the reactor framework and its implementations: ACE_Select_Reactor, ACE_TP_Reactor, ACE_WFMO_Reactor). Handlers derive from ACE_Event_Handler and expose handle_input/handle_timeout hooks; they register with an ACE_Reactor (register_handler), which demultiplexes with select, poll or WFMO and dispatches the hooks. Choose it when the surrounding stack is already ACE - its Acceptor-Connector, Service Configurator and Streams frameworks are built on the same reactor - and let the framework own rearming and handler lifetime instead of re-implementing them.
pitfalls: ACE ties handlers to its own frameworks and configuration; pulling in ACE for one loop is rarely worth it unless the Service Configurator/Acceptor-Connector stack is already in use.
ACE_TP_Reactor changes the single-thread guarantee: handlers may run concurrently on several threads, so handler state needs its own locking.
Handler destruction is managed by ACE reference counting and deactivation, so deleting a handler while it is still registered leaves the reactor dispatching through a dangling pointer.

variants.name: Hand-written epoll loop with a function-style handler table (no framework)
variants.idiom_name: epoll_wait loop + std::function handlers keyed by fd
variants.implementation_notes: Without a framework the C++ reactor is the C approach with better types: a std::unordered_map<int, std::function<void(uint32_t)>> (or a std::vector indexed by file descriptor) is the handler registry, epoll_wait is the demultiplexer, and the loop dispatches. std::function and lambdas remove the void-pointer context that the C version needs, and the same one-shot or edge-triggered rearm rules apply. Take this route when a dependency is not acceptable, when the reactor must own threads and affinities explicitly, or when the handles are foreign descriptors for which no framework service exists; otherwise the loop reimplements what Asio already ships.
pitfalls: Capturing by reference in the handler table keeps references to objects that may be destroyed while still registered; the classic C++ reactor bug is dispatch through a stale capture, so unregister before destruction and mind the iteration order.
std::function adds an indirection and a possible allocation on the hottest path; keep the table small, or store member-function pointers plus an object pointer where latency matters.
Readiness stays level-triggered unless the descriptor is registered with EPOLLET/EPOLLONESHOT, so handlers must drain or rearm exactly as in C.
